quote: Let us celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven.
firstReading: Paul rebukes the Corinthian community for tolerating a scandalous case of sexual immorality and for boasting instead of grieving. He commands the exclusion of the offender so that the community’s purity and witness are preserved. Paul insists that the church must judge those within its own fellowship and remove corruption to protect the whole. He frames the discipline in paschal terms: purge the old leaven so that, as new unleavened bread, the community may live in sincerity and truth.
psalmSummary: The psalmist contrasts the fate of the wicked and the righteous: God does not delight in evil or falsehood, and those who practice wickedness cannot stand in God’s presence. God thwarts the schemes of the wicked while giving refuge to the righteous. The faithful are promised God’s blessing and protection; the Lord surrounds the upright with favor as with a shield, vindicating and sustaining those who trust in him.
gospelSummary: In the synagogue on the sabbath, Jesus encounters a man with a withered hand while Pharisees watch to see whether he will heal, hoping to accuse him. Jesus addresses them with a moral question about doing good on the sabbath, then heals the man, restoring his hand. The healing provokes anger among the Pharisees, who begin to plot against Jesus. The episode contrasts Jesus’ compassion and authority with the hardness and legalism of his opponents, revealing the priorities of God’s law.
saintReflection: Saint Regina (Commemoration): Saint Regina, also known as Reine, is venerated as a virgin and martyr at Alise in Gaul, where devotion to her is attested from early centuries. The elaborate accounts of her childhood and trial are later traditions rather than secure historical biography; what endures is the Church's remembrance of her fidelity to Christ. Her witness directs attention to the freedom of a conscience bound to God and to the undivided love signified by consecrated virginity. Read in the light of Revelation's call to remain faithful unto death, her martyrdom expresses hope in the life Christ gives beyond the grave. She teaches through the witness of her remembrance rather than through surviving theological writings. Reflection on Regina invites prayer for purity of heart, perseverance under pressure, and the grace to confess the faith with courage, gentleness, and trust in God's final justice.
dailyPrayer: Lord Jesus, who heals with merciful power and calls your Church to truth and holiness, grant us hearts that refuse whatever would corrupt our communion. By your Spirit, help us to celebrate the paschal mystery with sincerity and truth, purging the old leaven of sin from our lives. Through the intercession of Saint Regina, give especially to the consecrated and to all the baptized the grace of pure affection for you, fidelity under trial, and a peaceful courage to confess your name. Make us instruments of compassion who, like you, choose to do good even when it draws opposition. Strengthen our trust in your final justice and in the life you give beyond the grave, that we may persevere until you come in glory. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis: The readings gather around discipline, mercy, and the right ordering of love. Paul’s call to cleanse the community is not triumphalist zeal but a pastoral move to preserve the integrity of the body of Christ so that its celebration of the paschal mystery is authentic. The psalm affirms God’s hatred of deceit and the divine protection of the righteous, a divine ordering that vindicates trust. In Luke, Jesus shows that Sabbath observance serves the life of persons; doing good and restoring wholeness fulfills the law’s purpose. Saint Regina’s remembered martyrdom exemplifies undivided love for Christ and a conscience shaped by fidelity. Together these texts invite a Church that is merciful yet watchful, holy yet compassionate, shaped by eschatological hope and steadfast witness.
exegesis:
Context: Paul writes to a community wrestling with disorder and a flawed moral imagination. In the passage read, he confronts an instance of grave sexual sin tolerated and even boasted about among the Corinthians. His vigorous response must be heard against the background of ancient communal identity: impurity in one member threatens the whole. Paul’s language of leaven and the festival of unleavened bread recasts the community’s life in liturgical terms, urging a moral and spiritual reform that corresponds to the paschal reality the Church celebrates.

Psalm: The psalm selection situates divine justice and protection at the center of faith. The Lord’s abhorrence of wickedness and falsehood stands as a theological counterweight to laxity; yet this is not mere retributive passion but the righteousness by which God distinguishes and sustains the faithful. The image of God blessing and shielding the upright offers consolation: the community that seeks righteousness will find divine favor even amid persecution and slander. The psalm thus supports the pastoral necessity of ordering the community so that the faithful may live under God’s protective favor.

Gospel: Luke’s narrative of Jesus healing on the sabbath casts a direct light on the law’s intention. Jesus faces opponents who watch for grounds to accuse him; by asking about doing good on the sabbath he exposes a moral inversion in their priorities. The healing of the man with a withered hand is not merely a miracle but a public declaration about the law’s servant role toward human flourishing. The violent reaction of the opponents, who begin to plot, reveals the cost of prophetic mercy: restoring life elicits resistance from those attached to a rigid, self-protective interpretation of law.

Saints: The remembrance of Saint Regina contributes a patristic and devotional angle to the day’s themes. Even where the details of her biography are later accretions, the Church’s preservation of her memory centers on fidelity unto death and the testimony of consecrated virginity. Regina’s witness exemplifies the single-hearted devotion Paul enjoins: an undivided love for Christ that will not compromise its allegiance. Her martyrdom, read in the light of Revelation and the paschal promise, expresses the hope that grounds endurance under persecution.

Theological Reflection: Bringing the readings and the saint together, a coherent theology emerges: holiness is both communal and personal, expressed in liturgical integrity, moral vigilance, and courage in witness. Paul’s severe pastoral action aims at resurrection life for the community; the psalm assures that God’s righteousness protects the upright; Luke shows that true observance of the law is measured by charity and the restoration of life. Regina’s example personalizes these claims: fidelity may demand costly witness, but it is ordered to the life Christ conquers in death.

Today: For the contemporary Church these texts call for sober discernment and pastoral charity. Discipline is not punitive isolation but a medicine tending toward conversion and communal health. Sabbath observance, prayer, and liturgical celebration must animate a life of mercy that prioritizes human dignity. The anniversary remembrance of a martyr invites the faithful to examine attachments that displace God and to pray for the grace of perseverance. In word and sacrament the Church is summoned to preserve truth with gentleness, to heal with courage, and to live in hope of the final vindication promised by Christ.

quote: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be Emmanuel.
firstReading: Micah 5:1-4a presents a prophetic portrait of Bethlehem as the unlikely birthplace of a ruler whose origins are from ancient times; though the town is small, from it will come a shepherd-king who will shepherd Israel and bring peace. The alternative reading, Romans 8:28-30, shifts to apostolic theology: God orders all things for the good of those he calls, effecting a sequence of calling, justification, and eventual glorification that discloses divine purpose for believers.
psalmSummary: Psalm 13:6ab,6c is an act of confident thanksgiving: the psalmist resolves to sing to the Lord because God has shown generous mercy. Even amid trial or feeling forsaken, the proper response is grateful praise for God’s faithful care; the verses express trust that God’s loving-kindness is the ground for hope and joyful song.
gospelSummary: Matthew 1:1-16 frames Jesus within Israel’s history by tracing a structured genealogy from Abraham through David to Joseph, stressing both continuity with the promises and the unexpected ways God works through human families. Verses 18-23 narrate Mary’s virginal pregnancy and Joseph’s struggle, resolved by an angelic message that the child is conceived by the Holy Spirit and is to be named Jesus, fulfilling the prophecy of a child called ‘Emmanuel,’ God-with-us. Matthew thus links Israel’s promise-keeping to the concrete reality of the Incarnation in Mary.
saintReflection: The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Feast): The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary celebrates the birth of the woman through whom the eternal Son of God would take human flesh. Scripture does not narrate Mary's birth, and later accounts of her childhood should be distinguished from the inspired Gospel. The feast instead contemplates her place within God's saving purpose: preserved from original sin by the grace of Christ, she was prepared to receive his Incarnation with free and faithful consent. The genealogy proclaimed in Matthew's Gospel places Jesus within Israel's history and culminates in his birth from Mary, affirming both God's fidelity to his promises and the reality of the Incarnation. Mary's holiness is entirely a gift of God, received in humility and expressed in obedience. Her nativity invites grateful reflection on grace, the dignity of human life, and the patient unfolding of divine salvation within human history.
dailyPrayer: Almighty Father, you began the work of our salvation in the hidden life of the Virgin Mary. We thank you for the gift of her birth, through which your eternal Word would one day take flesh. Grant that, following her example of humility and prompt obedience, we may welcome your will in our lives and cooperate with your grace. By the Spirit who overshadowed Mary, kindle in us faith that trusts your promises, hope that endures trials, and charity that bears faithful witness to Christ made man. Make us attentive to the voice of conscience and ready to say yes when you call. Through the intercession of Mary, Mother of God and Mother of the Church, bring to fulfillment in us the good that you have begun, for the glory of your name. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis: The readings together direct attention to God’s patient work in history and the singular role of Mary within that economy. Matthew’s genealogy situates Jesus in the line of promise, while the prophecy of a Bethlehem ruler (Micah) and the angel’s word to Joseph make explicit that God’s saving action culminates in a particular child born of a woman. Romans articulates the divine ordering that brings the called to justification and glorification. The feast of Mary’s nativity emphasizes that her holiness is a gift of prevenient grace: God prepares human freedom to receive the Incarnation. Thus the celebration affirms both divine initiative and human assent, the dignity of human life, and the faithful unfolding of salvation in history.
exegesis:
Context: The liturgical celebration of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary invites attention to the contours of salvation history. Matthew’s infancy material answers Matthew’s theological program: to show Jesus as the fulfillment of covenantal promises and as God present among his people. The prophetic expectation of a Bethlehem ruler (Micah) and the New Testament proclamation that God’s plan moves believers from calling to glorification (Romans) frame the feast as a meditation on God’s fidelity across time. The human genealogy underscores continuity with Israel; the birth narrative highlights the decisive novelty of God’s entrance into human life through a woman.

Psalm: The brief psalm verses appointed for the day are a note of grateful response. They capture the posture appropriate to the mystery we celebrate: thankfulness for God’s bountiful dealings and a resolve to sing God’s praises. In the presence of wonders that exceed human merit, the Psalm reframes astonishment into confident singing. The liturgy places thanksgiving alongside announcement and prophecy so that doctrinal affirmation is joined to personal praise.

Gospel: Matthew’s twofold infancy sequence — the genealogy and the narrative of Mary and Joseph — ties Jesus’ identity to Israel’s story while foregrounding God’s initiative. The genealogy is not a mere list; it is a theological map showing how the promise-bearing line culminates in Joseph’s legal fatherhood and in Mary’s maternal role. Matthew emphasizes fulfillment language: the prophecy of a one called Emmanuel is applied to the child of Mary. The angel’s message to Joseph resolves the scandal of an unexpected pregnancy by attributing conception to the Holy Spirit, thereby protecting both Mary’s chastity and the uniqueness of the Incarnation.

Saints: The feast is not a historical chronicle of Mary’s infancy; later narratives about her childhood must be distinguished from canonical witness. The liturgy, following sound tradition, concentrates on Mary’s place in salvation history. The Church has long reflected that Mary’s vocation was prepared by grace: she is understood as preserved and prepared by God to receive the Word. This is expressed not as human credit but as the fruit of divine generosity, leading to her free and faithful consent at the Annunciation.

Christological and theological connections: The readings together draw a line from promise to presence. Micah’s localizing of the ruler in Bethlehem finds its decisive fulfillment in Matthew’s narrative. Romans supplies the theology of divine ordering so that such fulfillment is seen not as chance but as the outworking of God’s saving plan. Mary’s nativity is thus celebrated as a hinge moment: through her, the Word assumes human nature. The Church’s teaching about Mary’s preparation and holiness must be read christocentrically — every claim about her is related to the unique work of Christ and the gift of grace that precedes human cooperation.

Today: For the faithful, the feast invites two practical stances. First, gratitude: celebrate God’s patient fidelity and give thanks as the psalm urges. Second, imitation: seek docility to grace so that God’s designs may find a human ‘yes.’ The nativity of Mary also prompts reflection on the dignity of human life from its beginning and on the mysterious economy by which God chooses ordinary human history to reveal his presence. In pastoral terms, the feast offers hope: God’s plans are patient, often hidden in humble circumstances, and they bear fruit when met by faithful consent.

quote: Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom.
firstReading: In 1 Corinthians 7:25–31 Paul addresses those unmarried during the present ‘distress,’ advising that, in light of urgent circumstances, they may remain as they are so as to serve the Lord without divided anxieties. Marriage and worldly ties are treated as legitimate but secondary; social arrangements are ephemeral. Paul emphasizes the transitory nature of present life and calls Christians to live with the Lord’s perspective, prioritizing fidelity to Christ over absorption in worldly concerns.
psalmSummary: Psalm 45:11–12, 14–15, 16–17 addresses a royal bride and celebrates her dignity, beauty, and honored standing beside the king. The psalm evokes royal marriage imagery—princes stand ready, the bride is led and adorned—and calls her to forget her people and home as she takes on a new covenantal role. The psalmist also prays that her name be remembered and praised within the nation, linking personal honor to the flourishing of God’s house.
gospelSummary: Luke 6:20–26 presents a striking set of beatitudes and corresponding woes. Jesus pronounces blessings on the poor, the hungry, those who weep, and the persecuted, promising the kingdom, satisfaction, comfort, and a great reward in heaven. He then issues woes against the rich, the well-fed, those who laugh now, and those praised by others, warning that current comforts may be reversed. Luke’s formulation emphasizes social reversal: God’s reign elevates the lowly and judges complacent privilege, calling disciples to solidarity with the vulnerable and fidelity amid opposition.
saintReflection: Saint Peter Claver (Memorial): Saint Peter Claver (1580–1654), a Jesuit priest from Spain, spent his ministry in Cartagena among Africans subjected to the brutality of the slave trade. He met arriving ships, attended to immediate bodily needs, and offered instruction in the faith and sacramental care. His ministry placed the suffering person, rather than social status, at the center of his attention. The theological principle is fundamental: every human being possesses dignity as God's creature, and Baptism unites people of every nation in the one Body of Christ. His care can be read alongside Jesus' identification with the vulnerable in Matthew 25 and Paul's teaching that all are one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). Claver's witness invites a conversion that refuses indifference to dehumanization. Reverence for Christ requires mercy toward those who suffer and a faith expressed through patient, concrete service.
dailyPrayer: Lord Jesus, you who opened your blessing to the poor and the sorrowing, grant us hearts that see human dignity in every face. Through the intercession of Saint Peter Claver, inflame our charity so that we tend to both the immediate needs and the spiritual care of those who suffer. Free us from complacency and the distractions of worldly gain; make us courageous in comforting the afflicted and patient in offering instruction and sacramental consolation. Unite us more deeply in Baptism to all your people, that our service become a sign of your kingdom. Help us to resist dehumanization wherever it appears and to work for justice with reverence and mercy. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis: The readings shape a common summons: discipleship orders life toward the reign of God rather than worldly comfort. Paul’s counsel to live unentangled by worldly anxieties highlights urgency and undivided service to the Lord. The Psalm’s royal-marriage imagery recalls covenantal dignity and public remembrance bestowed by God. Luke’s beatitudes turn human values upside down, promising God’s kingdom to the poor and warning the complacent rich. Saint Peter Claver’s ministry embodies this vision: he placed the suffering person at the center, treating every baptized person as a member of Christ’s Body. The theological through-line is baptismal dignity and merciful service—faith that recognizes Christ in the vulnerable and acts concretely to uphold their human and sacramental worth.
exegesis:
Context: Paul’s brief exhortation in 1 Corinthians 7:25–31 must be read within his broader pastoral concern for those living in a time he calls the “present distress.” He does not lay down an absolute rule but offers pragmatic guidance: to remain as one is can better secure undivided attention to the Lord. For Paul, the Christian’s horizon is shaped by eschatological urgency. Marriage and social relationships remain honorable, yet they carry obligations that can distract from serving Christ amid pressing circumstances. The passage insists on a freedom of heart that places fidelity to the Lord’s purposes above status or temporal advantage.

Psalm: Psalm 45’s selected verses employ nuptial and courtly language to celebrate honor and beauty within a royal context. Addressed to a bride, the psalm anticipates her entry into a new household and the public acknowledgment of her name. The royal marriage becomes a locus for covenantal identity: to be taken into the court is to be remembered and praised. The psalm thus affirms personal dignity tied to divine blessing and communal remembrance, underscoring how God’s favor lifts up those entrusted to his care.

Gospel: Luke 6:20–26 frames Jesus’ teaching by announcing blessings upon the poor, hungry, those who mourn, and the persecuted, paired with woes against the complacent and prosperous. Luke’s formulation stresses social reversal: God’s reign vindicates the lowly and exposes the danger of worldly security. Each beatitude promises not merely consolation but an eschatological reward—“the kingdom,” “satisfied,” “comforted,” “a great reward in heaven.” The corresponding woes function as prophetic warnings, calling the hearer to solidarity with those on the underside of society and fidelity that will cost the disciple persecution.

Saints: Saint Peter Claver’s ministry in Cartagena gives concreteness to these scriptural dynamics. His care for Africans trafficked in slavery placed immediate, embodied service at the center: meeting ships, tending wounds, administering sacraments, and offering catechesis. Claver’s witness enacts the beatitudinal preference for the poor and the Pauline insistence on living for the Lord rather than worldly gain. The theological principle emphasized in his life—that every person bears inalienable dignity as God’s creature and that Baptism unites people of every nation in Christ’s Body—translates scriptural truth into pastoral praxis. His ministry invites conversion from indifference, insisting that reverence for Christ requires mercy toward those who suffer.

Today: The convergence of these readings and Saint Peter Claver’s example challenges contemporary Christians in concrete ways. The Gospel’s reversal of values asks the Church to measure success not by wealth or reputation but by fidelity to the poor and persecuted. Paul’s counsel warns against allowing present comforts to undermine single-minded service to the Lord. The Psalm’s affirmation of public honor points toward a sacramental and communal remembering of those whom society would forget. Practically, this means prioritizing pastoral outreach, sacramental care, and advocacy for those dehumanized by structures of exploitation. The Christian response is not an abstract sentiment but a sustained, patient, and sacramental involvement in the lives of the vulnerable.

Conclusion: Together the texts and Saint Peter Claver’s life form a coherent summons: live with an eschatological horizon, honor the dignity of every baptized person, and let mercy guide concrete service. The Church’s vocation is to embody the beatitudes, to remember and praise those brought into God’s covenant, and to resist complacency when human dignity is denied. Such fidelity is at once theological—grounded in Baptism and the kingdom—and eminently practical, realized in patient, sacramental care for those who suffer.

quote: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you.
firstReading: Paul stresses that true wisdom is not mere knowledge but love. While acknowledging that ‘an idol is nothing’ and that food does not make us spiritually better or worse, he warns that exercising freedom can harm a weaker brother or sister. If one’s liberty leads another to stumble, charity requires self-restraint. He affirms that God’s gifts are meant for thanksgiving and the good of the community, and prudence demands foregoing rights to preserve another’s faith.
psalmSummary: The psalmist prays to the God who intimately knows every step and thought, who formed us in the womb. God’s knowledge is personal and searching: nothing is hidden from divine sight. The text rejoices in being fearfully and wonderfully made and invites God to examine the heart, to know any waywardness, and to lead in the way everlasting. It is a prayer for conversion rooted in God’s creative and discerning love.
gospelSummary: In Luke 6:27–38 Jesus calls disciples to a radical ethic of love and mercy: love enemies, bless and do good to those who hate you, turn the other cheek, and give without expectation of return. He exhorts non-retaliation and compassionate generosity: lend without counting on repayment. Jesus links mercy to the measure we employ toward others—do not judge, forgive, and you will receive forgiveness. His teaching culminates in the reciprocity of mercy: give and it will be given to you, for God’s generous measure meets our charity.
saintReflection: Saint Nicholas of Tolentino (Commemoration): Saint Nicholas of Tolentino (1245–1305) was an Augustinian priest who devoted himself to preaching, prayer, the Eucharist, and compassionate care for those in need. His ascetical discipline was joined to charity, showing that fasting is ordered toward freedom from sin and greater love of God and neighbor. He is especially remembered for prayer on behalf of the faithful departed, a devotion grounded in the communion of saints and the Church's hope in Christ's victory over death. Such intercession expresses confidence that God's purifying mercy prepares the faithful for the fullness of his presence. Nicholas' life therefore unites repentance, sacramental worship, and concern for souls. His example commends perseverance in prayer, tenderness toward the suffering, and remembrance of the dead, keeping the Eucharistic sacrifice of Christ at the heart of Christian hope.
dailyPrayer: Lord Jesus, Teacher of mercy, grant us the grace to love as you love. Where we are tempted to assert our rights, form our hearts to choose compassion; where knowledge tempts us to pride, grant us humility that puts the good of our neighbor first. May your Spirit root out judgment and cultivate forgiveness, so that we might reflect your merciful measure to the world. Through the intercession of Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, help us to remember the dead in prayer and to place the Eucharist at the center of our hope. Cleanse our hearts by your searching presence, heal what sin has broken, and send us forth to be instruments of your peace and charity. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis: The readings present a coherent moral vision centered on charity ordered by mercy. Paul insists that knowledge without love risks harming the vulnerable; true freedom is restrained by concern for others. The psalm grounds moral formation in God’s intimate knowledge and creative care, inviting interior conversion. Luke’s Gospel gives concrete practices—love of enemies, forgiveness, non-judgment, and generous giving—rooted in God’s own mercy. Saint Nicholas models these truths in a life of asceticism disciplined to charity, Eucharistic devotion, and intercession for the dead, showing that fasting, prayer, and sacramental worship serve the communion of saints and the ministry of mercy. Together they call the Church to a charity that preserves souls, forgives injuries, and mirrors God’s measure.
exegesis:
Context: Paul writes to a community divided about food offered to idols and the proper use of Christian liberty. In 1 Corinthians 8 he balances doctrinal clarity—an idol has no reality before God—with pastoral concern. The Corinthian situation is a test case: what one may rightly do in conscience can wound another’s faith. Paul insists that love must govern freedom; knowledge that does not build up but causes scandal contradicts the Gospel’s end, which is the salvation of souls.

Reading: The selected verses begin by correcting a presumptive boast in knowledge and point toward love as the determining ethic. Paul’s logic is simple but profound: knowledge may tell us that meat sacrificed to idols has no spiritual effect, but love regards the weaker brother whose conscience cannot distinguish. To avoid leading the weak to sin, the stronger should abstain. Paul thereby elevates the communal life of the Church above individual rights. Christian freedom is not an assertion of privilege but a service of charity.

Psalm: Psalm 139 situates moral formation in the reality of God’s penetrating knowledge and creative intimacy. ‘‘You search me, O Lord, and you know me’’ (vv.1–3) becomes the ground for conversion: if God knows the heart and formed us in the womb, then moral choices cannot be merely external acts. The psalmist’s appeal—‘‘Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my thoughts’’—invites purification by the One who is both creator and judge. This divine scrutiny fosters humility and dependence rather than self-sufficiency.

Gospel: Luke 6:27–38 sets forth the distinctive ethics of the Kingdom. Jesus calls for a love that surpasses conventional reciprocity—love even enemies, bless those who curse, and repay violence with non-retaliation. The passage links individual acts (turning the other cheek, giving without expecting return) to interior virtues: mercy and non-judgment. The reciprocity Jesus promises—‘‘forgive and you will be forgiven; give and it will be given to you’’—is not a transactional rule but an announcement that God’s mercy is the horizon of moral life. The ‘‘measure you use’’ summons the disciple to mirror divine generosity.

Saints: Saint Nicholas of Tolentino embodies the readings’ synthesis. His ascetic discipline, directed toward freedom from sin, aligns with Paul’s insistence that practices like fasting be ordered toward charity rather than self-display. Nicholas’s devotion to the Eucharist places sacramental worship at the heart of moral transformation, while his prayers for the departed express the communal continuity of charity—love that cares for souls beyond this life. His tenderness toward the suffering shows how Gospel commands become concrete service: he did not theorize mercy but enacted it. His memorial therefore illumines how personal sanctity and pastoral sensitivity cohere.

Today: The texts confront contemporary temptations to prioritize rights, knowledge, or performance over neighborly care. The challenge is pastoral and spiritual: to allow God’s searching love to form consciences that prefer the salvation of others. In communities fractured by difference, Paul’s counsel calls for restraint and solidarity; the psalm’s prayer asks God to make our inward life transparent to his healing; Luke’s commands turn conscience toward radical mercy. Saint Nicholas models perseverance in prayer and sacramental fidelity as means by which this conversion is sustained.

Application: Pastoral leaders and faithful alike are urged to cultivate a charity that both refrains from harmful liberty and actively forgives. Practically, this may mean choosing temperance in asserting legitimate freedoms, seeking reconciliation where judgment has hardened hearts, and remembering the dead in prayer as an act of ongoing charity. The Eucharist nourishes this life of mercy, making us able to love enemies and give without calculation. In hearing these readings, the Church is summoned to witness God’s measure of mercy so that the community itself becomes a place where souls are built up and led to fullness in Christ.
